main.title: Assassination of John F. Kennedy
main.summary: John F. Kennedy was assassinated in Dallas, Texas, on November 22, 1963, while travelling in a presidential motorcade.

cards.heading: Assassination of John F. Kennedy
cards.text:
On Friday, November 22, 1963, John F. Kennedy, the 35th president of the United States, was assassinated while riding in a presidential motorcade through Dallas, Texas. Kennedy was in the vehicle with First Lady Jacqueline Kennedy, Texas governor John Connally, and Connally's wife Nellie, when he was fatally shot from the nearby Texas School Book Depository by Lee Harvey Oswald, a former U.S. Marine. The motorcade rushed to Parkland Memorial Hospital, where Kennedy was pronounced dead about 30 minutes after the shooting; Connally was also wounded in the attack but recovered. Vice President Lyndon B. Johnson was hastily sworn in as president two hours and eight minutes later aboard Air Force One at Dallas Love Field.

After the assassination, Oswald returned home to retrieve a pistol; he shot and killed a lone Dallas policeman J. D. Tippit shortly afterwards. Around 70 minutes after Kennedy and Connally were shot, Oswald was apprehended by the Dallas Police Department and charged under Texas state law with the murders of Kennedy and Tippit.

main.title: 8½
main.subtitle: A filmmaker cannot find the film he is supposed to make
main.summary: Federico Fellini's 8½ follows Guido Anselmi, a celebrated director unable to bring his next film into focus. Marcello Mastroianni plays a man surrounded by people expecting decisions while he retreats into memories and fantasies. Released in 1963, the film makes the difficulty of creating a work the material from which that work is built.

cards.heading: A film about making a film
cards.text: Federico Fellini's 8½ follows Guido Anselmi, a celebrated director unable to bring his next film into focus. Marcello Mastroianni plays a man surrounded by people expecting decisions while he retreats into memories and fantasies. Released in 1963, the film makes the difficulty of creating a work the material from which that work is built.

cards.heading: The production follows Guido
cards.text: Guido visits a spa hoping to rest, but producers, performers and people from his private life soon gather around him. Questions about casting and the production mingle with conflicts involving his wife and mistress. The film moves into childhood recollections and imagined encounters without making them feel like separate exercises. Each diversion shows something Guido cannot settle in an ordinary conversation. His inner life keeps interrupting the orderly account that the people around him demand.

cards.heading: Order inside the confusion
cards.text: Gianni Di Venanzo's black-and-white photography and Piero Gherardi's sets and costumes give these shifts a precise visual setting. Crowded rooms, luminous faces and the exposed structures of a film production belong to the same unstable world. Nino Rota's music helps bring its many figures together. The film won the foreign-language Oscar and the award for Gherardi's black-and-white costume design, recognising both its imaginative construction and the detailed craft that makes that construction visible.

main.title: March on Washington
main.summary: Around 250,000 people gathered in Washington on 28 August 1963 to demand civil and economic rights for African Americans.

cards.heading: March on Washington
cards.text: Around 250,000 people gathered in Washington on 28 August 1963 to demand civil and economic rights for African Americans. Bayard Rustin and A. Philip Randolph organised an alliance of civil-rights, labour and religious groups around jobs and freedom. Singers including Mahalia Jackson and Marian Anderson performed, and movement leaders addressed the crowd. Martin Luther King Jr. spoke last before the Lincoln Memorial, calling for an end to legalised racism and segregation in his I Have a Dream speech. The march brought these demands before a national audience.

main.title: Please Please Me
main.summary: The Beatles released their debut album, Please Please Me, on 22 March 1963 through Parlophone.

cards.heading: Please Please Me
cards.text: The Beatles released their debut album, Please Please Me, on 22 March 1963 through Parlophone. George Martin produced its fourteen tracks, combining covers with Lennon–McCartney originals. After the success of the band's first singles, Martin considered a live recording but found Liverpool's Cavern Club unsuitable. A straightforward studio album followed instead: the main session took place at EMI Studios on 11 February, with overdubs added to Misery and Baby It's You nine days later. The record captured a band moving rapidly from singles to a full-length release.

main.title: Sketchpad
main.summary: Ivan Sutherland's 1963 Sketchpad pioneered interactive computer graphics and became a foundation for computer-aided design.

cards.heading: Sketchpad
cards.text: Sketchpad (a.k.a. Robot Draftsman) is a computer program written by Ivan Sutherland in 1963 in the course of his PhD thesis, for which he received the Turing Award in 1988, and the Kyoto Prize in 2012. It pioneered human–computer interaction (HCI), and is considered the ancestor of modern computer-aided design (CAD) programs and as a major breakthrough in the development of computer graphics in general. For example, Sketchpad inspired the graphical user interface (GUI) and object-oriented programming. Using the program, Sutherland showed that computer graphics could be used for both artistic and technical purposes and for demonstrating a novel method of human–computer interaction.

main.title: BASIC
main.summary: BASIC (Beginner's All-purpose Symbolic Instruction Code) is a family of general-purpose, high-level programming languages designed for ease of use.

cards.heading: BASIC
cards.text:
BASIC (Beginner's All-purpose Symbolic Instruction Code) is a family of general-purpose, high-level programming languages designed for ease of use. The original version was created by John G. Kemeny and Thomas E. Kurtz at Dartmouth College in 1964. They wanted to enable students in non-scientific fields to use computers. At the time, nearly all computers required writing custom software, which only scientists and mathematicians tended to learn.

In addition to the programming language, Kemeny and Kurtz developed the Dartmouth Time-Sharing System (DTSS), which allowed multiple users to edit and run BASIC programs simultaneously on remote terminals. This general model became popular on minicomputer systems like the PDP-11 and Data General Nova in the late 1960s and early 1970s. Hewlett-Packard produced an entire computer line for this method of operation, introducing the HP2000 series in the late 1960s and continuing sales into the 1980s. Many early video games trace their history to one of these versions of BASIC.

main.title: Civil Rights Act
main.summary: Signed on July 2, 1964, the Civil Rights Act outlawed discrimination in public accommodations, schools and employment.

cards.heading: Civil Rights Act
cards.text:
The Civil Rights Act of 1964 (Pub. L. 88–352, 78 Stat. 241, enacted July 2, 1964) is a landmark civil rights and labor law in the United States that outlaws discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, and national origin. It prohibits unequal application of voter registration requirements, racial segregation in schools and public accommodations, and employment discrimination. The act is considered one of the most significant legislative achievements in American history.

Initially, powers given to enforce the act were weak, but these were supplemented during later years. Congress asserted its authority to legislate under several different parts of the United States Constitution, principally its enumerated power to regulate interstate commerce under the Commerce Clause of Article I, Section 8, its duty to guarantee all citizens equal protection of the laws under the 14th Amendment, and its duty to protect voting rights under the 15th Amendment.

main.title: The first computer-mouse prototype
main.summary: Douglas Engelbart's team built its first computer-mouse prototype in 1964, translating movement over a surface into an on-screen pointer.

cards.heading: The first computer-mouse prototype
cards.text: Douglas Engelbart's team built its first computer-mouse prototype in 1964, translating movement over a surface into an on-screen pointer. Two wheels tracked motion in separate directions, giving the hand a way to control a computer display. Engelbart demonstrated the device publicly in 1968 during the event later known as The Mother of All Demos. Subsequent designs used a rolling ball and then optical detection. The underlying relationship stayed familiar: moving a small object on a desk could move a pointer through a graphical interface.

main.title: Dr. Strangelove
main.summary: Stanley Kubrick's 1964 black comedy follows a nuclear command system struggling to stop an unauthorised attack.

cards.heading: Dr. Strangelove
cards.text: Stanley Kubrick's Dr. Strangelove turned the fear of nuclear war into black comedy in 1964. A paranoid American general orders an attack on the Soviet Union, leaving the president and military officials trying to stop a B-52 crew from carrying it out. Peter Sellers plays three roles, including the president and the scientific adviser Dr. Strangelove. Kubrick wrote the screenplay with Terry Southern and Peter George, loosely adapting George's thriller Red Alert. The resulting satire follows a command system struggling with the destructive consequences of its own operation.

main.title: IBM System/360
main.summary: The IBM System/360 (S/360) is a family of computer systems announced by IBM on April 7, 1964, and delivered between 1965 and 1978.

cards.heading: IBM System/360
cards.text: The IBM System/360 (S/360) is a family of computer systems announced by IBM on April 7, 1964, and delivered between 1965 and 1978. System/360 was the first family of computers designed to cover both commercial and scientific applications and a complete range of sizes from small, entry-level machines to large mainframes. The design distinguished between architecture and implementation, allowing IBM to release a suite of compatible designs at different prices. All but the only partially compatible Model 44 and the most expensive systems use microcode to implement the instruction set, which used 8-bit byte addressing with fixed-point binary, fixed-point decimal and hexadecimal floating-point calculations. The System/360 family introduced IBM's Solid Logic Technology (SLT), which packed more transistors onto a circuit card, allowing more powerful but smaller computers, but did not include integrated circuits, which IBM considered too immature.
